title: The Agreement Every Board and CEO Should Make
author: Managing the Future
summary: Managing the Future argues that most tension between CEOs and boards is not about the content of decisions but about undocumented ambiguity over who makes them. The solution is a simple Board-CEO Operating Agreement—one or two pages written down—that makes explicit the existing assumptions about spending authority, hiring decisions, and strategic initiative boundaries. Without this document, both sides fill the gap with different mental models, and the resulting surprises erode the trust that CEO effectiveness depends on.
points: Governance documents cover decisions reserved to the board by law but say nothing about the dozens of consequential judgment calls a CEO makes every month—that gap is where trust is built or lost.

A Board-CEO Operating Agreement is not a legal document but a written understanding of how the company will actually be run, making implicit assumptions explicit so both sides discover where they agree and where they don't.
CEOs without this framework tend toward two failure modes: checking in on everything (signalling insecurity) or acting unilaterally on issues the board expected to weigh in on (eroding trust).
Vague terms like 'material expenditure' invite different interpretations from every person at the table; dollar thresholds and specific examples remove the ambiguity that produces unwanted surprises.
Boards hate surprises above almost anything else; a CEO who regularly brings news of decisions the board thought they'd be consulted on will eventually lose the board's confidence.
Once expectations are written down, both sides spend less time guessing and more time focused on what they are actually there to do: build and run a healthy business.
quotes: They include dollar thresholds for spending, guidance around hiring executives, examples of strategic decisions that require board involvement, and the types of governance decisions that always remain with the board.

There are few things boards hate more than surprises, and if you regularly walk into board meetings with news of decisions you made that the directors think they should’ve had a say in, you’re asking for trouble.
Material expenditure” sounds precise until everyone around the table realizes they have a different definition of “material.” A dollar amount doesn’t leave much room for interpretation.
Once these expectations and guidelines are written down, both sides spend less time guessing and more time focusing on what they are there to do: build and run a healthy business.
This way, you’re not left trying to get everything rubber stamped or put in a situation where the board is thrown off by you getting out over your skis—at least as they see it.
That is the territory where trust is actually built or lost, and there is usually little specificity on where the boundary between CEO authority and board authority lies.
